Naloxone (often called Narcan), is an opioid antagonist medication. It is used to reverse the effects of opioid painkillers, especially when a person has overdosed on opioids. Examples of opioids include morphine, oxycodone (often called Percocet when mixed with acetaminophen, OxyIR, or OxyContin), hydrocodone (often called Vicodin when mixed with acetaminophen), methadone and meperidine (Demerol or pethidine). The effects of these drugs can make it hard for the person to speak and there is no downside to giving someone a dose of naloxone if it is thought that they are having an overdose. These painkillers are central nervous system depressants. This means they slow down certain areas of the brain. If a person takes too many opiates, this can shut down the part of the brain that controls the voluntary organs such as the diaphragm. This can make them stop breathing. Naloxone may be mixed into the same pill as an opioid painkiller to decrease the risk of misuse. When a person has taken too much of one of these painkillers, naloxone can reverse the painkillers' effects and save the person's life. When given intravenously, naloxone works within two minutes. When injected into a muscle, it works within five minutes. The medication may also be shot up the nose and this is how it is used the most often. The effects of naloxone last about 30 minutes to an hour. Since most opioids last longer than naloxone, a person may need several doses of naloxone to fight the effects of an overdose. When a person takes opioids, the opioids have to attach to certain receptor sites in the brain in order to work, like a lock's key in a keyhole. Once the opioids attach to these opiate receptor sites - like a lock's key fitting into a keyhole - the opiates start to work. Opiates and opioids also act on other receptors. They block pain, create euphoria, and make people feel calm and relaxed. But if a person takes too many opiates or too much, that can also make it impossible to breathe, for example when the diaphragm (a muscle) relaxes too much along with the other muscles. Naloxone fits better onto these opiate receptor sites than actual opiates do. It is an opioid antagonist. If a person takes naloxone, the naloxone will throw any opiate off of the opiate receptor sites (like a key getting taken out of a door). Naloxone will stay attached to these opiate receptor sites. This reverses the effects of the opiates that the person took. Naloxone reverses the effects of opiates. Because of this, if a person who is addicted to opiates gets naloxone, they will have symptoms of opioid withdrawal. People have withdrawal symptoms when their body gets used to having opiates all the time. Because naloxone reverses the effects of opiates, the side effects of naloxone can include restlessness, agitation, nausea, vomiting, a fast heart rate, pain, and sweating. To prevent this, small doses every few minutes can be given until the desired effect is reached. Naloxone has to be given carefully to people with heart disease. Naloxone can cause more heart problems, like changes in the rhythm of the heart beat, in these people. Naloxone seems to be safe in pregnant women. Naloxone is a pure opioid antagonist. In rare cases, naloxone can cause adverse effects like seizures and pulmonary edema (fluid in the lungs). Naloxone was patented in 1961 by Jack Fishman, Mozes J. Lewenstein, and the company Daiichi Sankyo. The drug was approved for opioid overdose by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 1971. It is on the World Health Organization's Model List of Essential Medicines, the most important medications needed in a basic health system. Naloxone is available as a generic medication and is not very expensive. Its wholesale price (as of 2015) is between $0.50 and $5.30 USD per dose. Naloxone can be used to reverse opioid overdose and to reduce the slowed breathing or mental depression that opioids can cause. Naloxone is included as a part of emergency overdose response kits distributed to heroin and other opioid drug users. This has been shown to reduce deaths due to overdose. A prescription for naloxone is recommended if a person is: On a high dose of opioid (over 100 mg of morphine a day, or an equal amount of another opiate); Is prescribed any dose of opioid along with a benzodiazepine; or If naloxone is prescribed to a person, that person should also be taught about how to prevent, identify, and react to an overdose, including how to perform rescue breathing, CPR, and how to call an emergency telephone number like 9-1-1. Naloxone may be mixed with a number of opioids like buprenorphine. (Buprenorphine mixed with naloxone is called Suboxone.) Buprenorphine is used to decrease cravings for opiates. When buprenorphine and naloxone are mixed, and taken by mouth, only buprenorphine has an effect. But if a person misuses Suboxone by injecting it or taking large doses, the naloxone blocks the effect of the opioid. This combination is used to try to prevent abuse.

In general relativity, a naked singularity is a gravitational singularity that is viewable from anywhere in the outside area. The event horizon is like a bubble which surrounds a black hole. Inside the event horizon, the pull of the light cannot escape, so we are unable to view objects inside the event horizon. This includes the event horizon itself. Naked singularities do not have an event horizon, hence the term 'naked'. The existence of naked singularities is a very important topic in physics, because it would mean we could actually see phenomena made by black holes that we wouldn't be able to see otherwise. In addition, naked singularities would pose big problems for general relativity, since scientists still have not figured out a working idea for what happens to space-time in and around a black hole. Quantum mechanics, the main other scientific theory scientists turn to in physics, is also unable to explain how space-time would behave in such a situation. Although the cosmic censorship hypothesis says that naked singularities cannot exist, some research says that if loop quantum gravity (a scientific theory that says the universe is made of small 'loops') is correct, naked singularities could exist in nature. Other calculations and arguments have been made to support this. There are black holes known as Kerr black holes which have spin (they rotate). But, there is a maximum spin rate. If it spins faster than that maximum, its horizon disappears, leaving the singularity inside it wide open. Mathematician Demetrios Christodoulou has shown that naked singularities also occur in nature. However, he then showed that such "naked singularities" are unstable.

On 8 and 9 February 2020, a mass shooting happened in Nakhon Ratchasima Province (also known as Korat) in Thailand. A soldier killed 29 people at four locations. He started the attack on 8 February at a house, where he killed two people. He then went to a military camp, where he killed a soldier. Later on 8 February, he went to the city of Nakhon Ratchasima, where he killed 9 people at a Buddhist temple. Over a period of hours, he killed 17 people in a shopping mall. The soldier was shot and killed by the police at the mall on 9 February.

The Nalchik concentration camp or ghetto was a concentration camp established by Nazi Germany in October or November of 1942. It is famous for its systematic torture and murder of inmates. The camp imprisoned Russian Jews (and people believed to be Jewish). The Nazis targeted people coming from the entire Caucausus Mountains area, not just Nalchik. The German officers in the camp called it "Jewish Colony." By January of 1943, the German officers at Nalchik had made a plan to exterminate all (or nearly all) of the prisoners in the camp. They planned to begin killing people on 4 January. Fortunately, on 3 January, Nalchik was liberated by a nearby Soviet Red Army military unit. The unit had been sent to liberate the city of Nalchik. Because the camp was liberated early, nearly all of the people imprisoned there survived. Around two hundred people were killed. Nalchik was occupied by Nazi Germany from 28 October 1942 to 3 January 1943. This was a short time compared to other areas like Poland and France, which were occupied for years. Unlike most other concentration camps, almost all of the inmates survived Nalchik, since it lasted just a few months. For these reasons, Holocaust historians and scholars were slow to recognize Nalchik survivors as "true" Holocaust survivors.

Nakivubo Channel is the main dirty water movement channel in Kampala, the capital city of Uganda. It is about nine kilometres long. The channel carries rainwater from many busy parts of the city and sends it toward Lake Victoria. It also collects water from smaller side drains, including the Jugula drainage line. For many years, Nakivubo Channel has been very important for Kampala’s drainage system, but it has also had many problems. It has often been blocked by rubbish, soil and waste. This has caused floods, bad smells and harm to the environment. Because of these problems, many people have talked about how to repair or improve the channel. In 2024, people again paid attention to the channel because new plans were made to improve it and cover some parts of it. These plans came after CAF said the area around the new Nakivubo Stadium needed to be safer and cleaner as Uganda prepared to host AFCON 2027. In April 2025, the Kampala Capital City Authority (KCCA) Council agreed that skilled local investors could help rebuild and cover important open drainage channels, as long as the work was guided and checked by KCCA’s technical teams. Later in the same year, businessman Hamis Kiggundu, through his company KIHAM Enterprises (U) Ltd, suggested a plan to make the Nakivubo Channel wider, cleaner and stronger, and to cover it as part of a project paid for with private money. The plan gained more support after a presidential directive (an order from the President) in August 2025, which told government offices to help the planned works go ahead. The plan is to cover the open channel and let the water move inside a strong underground system. This is meant to help rainwater move better, stop rubbish from blocking the channel, make the area safer for people and improve how the place looks. The plan also includes building tall commercial buildings on top of the covered parts of the channel so that the investor can get back the money spent on the project. As of 2025, the work is still going on in stages. Many people — including the public, engineers and environmental groups — are still watching and discussing the project. The Nakivubo drainage line was first built to carry rainwater from the crowded middle parts of Kampala. These areas include Makerere Kivulu, Bat Valley, Nakasero, Owino Market and the industrial area. Fast growth of the city, loss of wetlands and poor care over many years made the channel weaker and dirtier. By the 2000s and 2010s, the channel was full of soil, damaged in some places and often used as a dumping place for rubbish. This made floods more common in downtown areas such as Kikuubo, Clock Tower and Nakivubo Trading Centre. The Nakivubo wetland around the channel used to help clean dirty water before it reached Lake Victoria. Over time, people built houses and businesses on the wetland. This made the wetland much smaller. Because of this, it can no longer hold floodwater or clean the water as well as before. Kampala often has flooding, especially when it rains very heavily. Blocked inlets, small culverts, illegal dumping and building too close to drains have been named in government and World Bank reports as main reasons for drainage problems. Big floods in 2019, 2023 and 2025 damaged many businesses and public services. These floods increased public calls for better drainage systems in Kampala. The channel has also been linked to health risks. Water in the channel can contain plastics, faecal matter and industrial waste. The open channel has raised safety concerns, because some reports say that criminals have used it as a hiding place. The rebuilding of Nakivubo War Memorial Stadium in 2024 brought new attention to the channel. Inspections by the Confederation of African Football (CAF), FUFA and FIFA found that the stadium itself was strong enough, but they pointed out problems near it. These problems included open drains, rubbish and unsafe roads and paths around the stadium. After these inspections, workers cleared rubbish and removed mud and soil from the channel around the stadium. This helped water flow better for a short time. The condition of Nakivubo Channel later became one of the main issues in Uganda’s plans for co-hosting AFCON 2027. In early 2025, new plans were made to cover, widen and improve parts of the channel through work shared between government and private investors. The plans aimed to change the open trench into a strong underground drain and to build commercial buildings or public spaces on top. People who supported the plan said it would help reduce flooding, improve safety and make the surrounding city area look better. Critics worried about harm to the environment, how the project would be controlled and who would take care of this big public drainage channel in the future. In July 2025, businessman Dr. Hamis Kiggundu sent a formal proposal to President Yoweri Museveni explaining a plan to clean, widen, cover and rebuild the channel using private money. The proposal said that the open channel was a big cause of flooding, rubbish build-up and public health risks. It also said that building commercial projects on top of the covered channel would help pay for the works. On 2 August 2025, President Museveni issued a directive supporting the proposal and telling the Prime Minister and other ministries to help the project move forward. The order allowed the rebuilding to start and led to early works such as clearing the site and cleaning the drainage in mid-August 2025 under government supervision. Debates over the law, supervision and engineering design of the planned works continued. These debates involved Kampala Capital City Authority (KCCA), the Ministry for Kampala, Parliament, environmental authorities and State House. In April 2025, KCCA Council passed a formal decision allowing qualified private investors to rebuild and cover important open drainage channels, as long as KCCA supervised the work. Later in 2025, the National Environment Management Authority (NEMA) gave Environmental and Social Impact Assessment (ESIA) approval for one of the planned projects, but with conditions to reduce harm to people and nature. Parliamentary committees, including the Committee on Physical Infrastructure, visited the channel to check the works. Their reports noted some engineering improvements but also said that strong rules and proper compliance were still needed. Heavy rain on 31 October 2025 caused serious flooding in central Kampala. The floods affected arcades, shops and main transport routes. The incident increased public debate about the condition of the channel and whether the rebuilding works were enough. Government reports said that blocked culverts and inlets further upstream were key reasons for the flooding. The event also increased calls for wider drainage improvements across the whole city, not only at Nakivubo Channel. Nakivubo Channel is part of a larger wetland system that used to help clean Kampala’s dirty water before it reached Lake Victoria. Environmental groups and community organisations have warned that covering or changing the channel, without also improving waste collection and protecting the remaining wetlands, could make the environment weaker and less able to recover from problems. Concerns include losing what is left of the wetland functions, putting more pressure on man-made drainage systems, long-term environmental damage and questions about who will maintain the new structures. NEMA’s Environmental Social Impact Assessment approval included conditions and steps to reduce these risks. As of late 2025, work to improve the Nakivubo Channel is still going on in stages. Some parts of the channel have already been cleaned, widened or made stronger. Plans to cover some sections and build on top of them have also been approved by planning and environmental authorities.. Work continues under the oversight of KCCA, the Ministry for Kampala and national environmental authorities. The channel still carries rainwater, but it is also central to many important discussions about how Kampala should plan its city, deal with climate change, work with private investors and improve its drainage systems in the future.

Namaste or Namaskar is a neutral greeting used a lot in many East Asian countries. It is used when Hello and Hi are used in English, though it has a very different meaning. Namaste is kind of like a praise to the person receiving the namaste. The word's meaning is “I bow to the divine in you.” Namaste is a traditional Indian greeting of respect and thank you, with spiritual and symbolic meaning, This is more traditional to do it to your elders.

Namal Lake is in one corner of the Namal valley in Mianwali, Punjab, Pakistan. This lake was created when Namal Dam was constructed in 1913. Namal Dam is 32 km from Mianwali city. The lake has a surface area of 5.5 km². There are mountains on its western and southern sides. On the other two sides are agricultural areas. Namal Lake is an ideal abode for the migratory birds in winter season when thousands of water fowls, including Russian ducks and Siberian cranes, land in the lake water.
Nambé Pueblo is a federally recognized tribe of the Tewa Pueblo people in Santa Fe County, New Mexico. The United States Census Bureau has labeled the community as a census-designated place (CDP).

Numbers that are larger than one million are usually either shown using scientific notation, or by words. The words billion and trillion, and millions were first written to describe extremely large numbers in 1475 by Jehan Adam. In 1484, Nicolas Chuquet used the words million, billion, trillion, decillion, and even further to write and describe much larger numbers. For example, Adam's billion (Chuquet's (bi)llion) was used to write 1012. While these were the first writings that used these words, Adam and Chuquet were probably not the creators of the words. The word million comes from the Old Italian millione. These words were most likely used a lot before the books were written. (For "missing" numbers, like 10^26, say "100 Septillion") There is also the number googol, which is a 1 with 100 zeros behind it (10,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000), and the number googolplex, which is a 1 with a googol of zeros behind it, (1010,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000) (1010100). The number googolplexian, is a 1 with a googolplex number of zeros behind it (101010100). The name centillion was made in the 19th century for the 100th "illion", being 10303 in the short scale and 10600 in the long scale.

Naming very small numbers is the same as naming very big numbers, but with one important difference. There is a minus sign over what the 10 in the formula is raised to. So if one wanted to write 0.007 in shorthand form, they would write it 7 x 10−3 since 7 is the third digit after the decimal point (the zero in front of the decimal point does not count). Naming a very small number with lots of different numbers inside it is the same as doing it with a very big number, but again with that one difference of the minus sign. So 0.0000452 would become 4.52 x 10−5 (0.0000452 --> 4.52 x 0.00001 --> 4.52 x 10−5).

There are areas on the periodic table where elements have similar properties. Such areas include Groups, especially columns. For example, all of the first column elements (alkali metals) are light, very soft, react with water rapidly, make hydroxides that are strong bases, and react with the halogens to make colorless ionic compounds. The second column elements (alkaline earth metals) are a little heavier, a little harder, react with water a little less rapidly, made hydroxides that are strong bases, and react with the halogens to make colorless ionic compounds. The other categories are: transition metals, pnictogens, chalcogens, halogens, and noble gases. There are also inner transition metals that are divided into lanthanides and actinides.

Nami Hayakawa is an archer from Japan. She was born on 6 October 1984. Hayakawa competed at the 2008 Summer Olympics. During the 2008 Summer Olympics held in Beijing, Hayakawa completed her initial ranking round with a total of 649 points. This secured her the 9th position for the final competition bracket. In the first round, she faced off against Elena Mousikou and triumphed over the archer from Cyprus with a score of 112-103. In the second round, she exhibited her strength by defeating Jennifer Nichols with a score of 105-103, and she continued her journey by outscoring Naomi Folkard with 106-97 to reach the quarter-finals. Unfortunately, she was eliminated in the quarter-finals by Park Sung-hyun with a score of 112-103, who later went on to win the silver medal. Hayakawa participated in the team event alongside Sayoko Kitabatake and Yuki Hayashi. Their combined scores from the ranking round, including Hayakawa's 649 points, Kitabatake's 616, and Hayashi's 616, placed the Japanese team in the seventh position after the ranking round. In the first round of the team event, they defeated the Colombian team with a score of 206-199. However, in the quarter-finals, they faced a formidable opponent in second-seeded Great Britain, who outperformed Japan with a score of 201-196.

The Namibia Football Association (NFA) is the governing body of football in Namibia. It is in charge of the men's and the women's national teams. The association was founded in 1990. It became a member of FIFA and CAF in 1992.

India has two official names, India and Bharat. Both names are important because of history. Some North Indians also call it Hindustan when they talk to each other. People use "India," "Bharat," or "Hindustan" based on the situation and language they are speaking. The English term is from Greek Indikē (cf. Megasthenes' work Indica) or Indía, via Latin transliteration India. The Old Persian word for "Sindhu" was "Hindu." When King Darius I conquered Sindh around 516 BCE, the Persians called the region "Hindus." Scylax of Caryanda, an explorer working for the Persian emperor, likely introduced this name to Greek. In Herodotus’s *Geography*, the words "Indos" (for the Indus River) and "Indian" appear. The Greek dialects spoken in Asia Minor may have caused the loss of the /h/ sound. Herodotus also used "Indian" to describe all people east of Persia, even though he didn’t have a precise understanding of the geography. The term "Indies" originally referred to land east of the Indus River and was another way of saying "India." When the Portuguese explored new regions, they called them the Indies. The Caribbean islands were first called the "Indies" because explorers thought they had reached India. Later, when they realized these islands were in the western hemisphere, they renamed them the "West Indies," meaning "India in the west." Indonesia was once called the Dutch East Indies, meaning "India in Southeast Asia." This is different from "Dutch India," which referred to the trading posts of the Dutch East India Company in the Indian subcontinent. Bharat is another name for India, officially recognized in Article 1 of the Indian Constitution, which was adopted in 1950. The Constitution states in English: "India, that is Bharat..." The name Bharat was commonly used in Sanskrit and later became a self-chosen alternative name for India, embraced by many people in the Indian subcontinent. Bharat comes from the name of the Bharatas, a Vedic community mentioned in the Rigveda. They were one of the original groups in Āryāvarta and played a significant role in the Battle of the Ten Kings. The earliest known use of "Bhārata-varṣa" as a geographical term appears in the Hathigumpha inscription of King Kharavela from the first century BCE. In this inscription, the name refers to a limited region in northern India, specifically the part of the Ganges west of Magadha. It also states that Bharat was named after Bharata, the son of Rishabhanatha, the first Jain Tirthankara. The name "Hindus" was recorded in the Old Persian cuneiform script, used in Achaemenid inscriptions. It was written as "𐏃𐎡𐎯𐎢𐏁" (H-i-du-u-š). This script was used in various regions, including Egypt, where references to Hindus were also found in inscriptions from the Achaemenid era. (H-n-d-wꜣ-y) on the Statue of Darius I, circa 500 BCE. Emperor Babur of the Mughal Empire described India’s geography, saying, "On the East, the South, and the West it is bounded by the Great Ocean." The word "Hind" was adapted into Arabic as "Al-Hind" (الهند) to refer to India, as seen in historical works like the 11th-century *Tarikh Al-Hind* ("History of India"). The term still appears in India today, such as in the patriotic phrase "Jai Hind" (जय हिन्द) and in "Hind Mahāsāgar" (हिन्द महासागर), the Hindi name for the Indian Ocean. Jambudvīpa was an ancient name for India before "Bharath" became widely used. It may indirectly refer to Insular India. The term "Jambu Dwipa" was historically used in many Southeast Asian countries to refer to India before the English word "India" was introduced. Even today, it is sometimes used in Thailand, Malaysia, Java, and Bali to describe the Indian subcontinent, though it can also refer to all of Asia. Maurya Emperor Ashoka used this name in his inscriptions to describe his empire. Gyagar and Phagyul are old Tibetan names for India. In ancient times, Tibetan Buddhist writers and travelers used the word Gyagar to talk about India, especially the southern part. They used Madhyadesa for middle India. From the 1200s, Tibetans also started using the word Phagyul, short for Phags yul, which means "land of noble or enlightened people." The Tibetan scholar Gendun Chopel said that Gyagar comes from the Sanskrit word vihāra, which means a Buddhist monastery. Ancient Tibetans used Gyagar mainly for north and central India, from Kuru (now Haryana) to Magadha (now Bihar). The famous story Epic of King Gesar called India many names like "Gyagar, the land of Buddhist teachings," "Gyagar, the land of medicine," "Gyagar, the land of pearls," and "Gyagar, the land of golden vases." The Central Tibetan Administration says that Tibet and India have strong ties in history, culture, and religion. It calls India Gyagar Phagpay Yul, which means "India, the land of noble ones." The Dalai Lama calls India his teacher and says Tibet is its student. He also calls himself a "Son of India" and follows Mahatma Gandhi’s ideas. He continues to share India’s old wisdom, especially the Nalanda tradition of learning. Tianzhu (Chinese: 天竺) is an old Chinese name for India. The name comes from the Sanskrit word Sindhoo, which changed into Hindoo in Persian and was later written as Tianzhu in Chinese. Other East Asian countries also use similar words: Buddhists in China and nearby countries used the word Tianzhu to talk about India as a holy place, because Buddhism started there. They saw India as their "heavenly center" or sacred land. Other Chinese names for India appear in history books. Juāndú (身毒) is found in the Shiji by Sima Qian. Tiāndǔ (天篤) is used in the Book of the Later Han (Hou Hanshu) Another name is Yìntèjiā (印特伽), which comes from Indaka, an old form of the word Hindu used by the people of Kucha. Hodû (Hebrew: הֹדּוּ) is the name for India in the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament. It appears in the Book of Esther, chapters 1:1 and 8:9. In this book, King Ahasuerus (usually identified with Xerxes I of Persia) is said to have ruled over 127 provinces, from Hodû (India) to Ethiopia. The word Hodû probably comes from the Sanskrit word Sindhu, which means "great river", this refers to the Indus River. It came into Hebrew through the Old Persian word Hindu. So, "Hodu" and "India" are the same in meaning and origin.

The Nana Farari was a Koli revolutionary (later turned as Dacoit) from Bombay State (now Maharashtra) who fought against the British rule in India during Indian independence movement in 1947. Nana Ferrari was born in a Koli family of Maharashtra and even today stories of Nana Ferrari can be heard in Dharampur, Surgana and Peth towns of Maharashtra and Gujarat. Nana Farari took active part in Indian independence movement but after independence of India in 1947, Nana Farari continued his rebellion. Nana Farari took up arms against hoarding and malsaji Sahukars and Moneylenders, due to which in October 1947, Nana Farrari had cut off the nose and ears of the people from trading communities such as Bania, Parsi and Teli, due to which the Bombay State (present days Maharashtra) government declared Nana Farari as a dacoit despite revolutionary status in public. After this, For several months, Bombay state Police used to search Nana in Nashik and Trimbak to catch Nana Farari and one day in battle with police force, Nana Ferrari was killed in an encounter in Toragaon village.

The Nanakshahi calendar is a solar calendar used in Sikhism. It's based on the "Barah Maha" (Twelve months), a composition by Sikh gurus that talks about natureal changes in the twelve-month cycle of the year. The year starts with the month of Chet, and 1 Chet is on 14 March. The calendar's starting point is the birth of Guru Nanak Dev in 1469 CE.
